newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav business climate still gloomy - experts.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav business climate still gloomy - experts.

text.p: General insolvency, lack of working capital and huge public spending are still major obstacles to revival of Yugoslav economy, experts said on Wednesday.

"Despite slight improvement in April, the business climate is still quite unfavourable with shortage of cash being the main problem of the entire economy," Tomislav Milisavljevic, an expert of the Belgrade Market Research Institute (IZIT) said.
The relaxed central bank restrictivness and limited financial support to export-oriented production were the sole positive impetus to the economy, he said.
IZIT said money supply M1 by mid-April reached last December's level of some 5.6 billion dinars ($1.002 billion).
A sudden monetary expansion at the end of 1996 pushed the dinar's black market rate down to 4.3 dinars to the German mark against its official rate of 3.3 dinars.
"If M1 remains at this level, relative stability of prices and the dinar will be preserved," Milisavljevic said.
Monthly inflation in April slowed to just 0.1 percent, after rising 1.0 percent in March. Year-on-year April retail price index rose 22.7 percent against 26.4 percent in March.
But cash in circulation was still high accounting for 47 percent of M1, Milisavljevic said.
Commercial banks lending grew by 350 million dinars in the first half of April against 3.53 billion dinars end of March.
The number of insolvent firms fell by one percent in April to 22,361 companies compared to March, but their unpaid liabilities rose three percent reaching 8.191 billion dinars.
Some 21,676 firms were permanently insolvent and their unpaid liabilites stood at 8.031 billion dinars. These firms employ 582,165 out of the officially 2.018 million employed.
"High insolvency shows the economy is a loss-maker which cannot secure enough money even to keep the production going," said IZIT's director Jovan Todorovic.
Recently published analysis of the Institute for Economic Sciences, another leading think-tank, said companies suffered 8.75 billion dinars in aggregate net losses in 1996.
According to some estimates, economy incurred another five billion dinars in net loss by the end of April.
Experts agreed huge public spending and inadequate tax system were also to blame for the poor state of the economy.
"Public spending is disproportionate to the size of gross domestic product and it must be radically cut. It is one of major obstacles for revival of the economy," Todorovic said.
Budget and social security funds' revenues in real terms grew 7.5 percent in April to 3.562 billion dinars against March and were up 6.1 percent on April last year.
Cumulative January-April revenues stood at 12.699 billion dinars, up five percent in real terms against the 1996 period.
"But the problem is their reallocation which is to the advantage of budget revenues," Todorovic said.
In real terms budget revenues were up 9.5 percent against the previous month and up 15 percent on April last year.
At the same time, revenues for social security funds in real terms grew 4.4 percent on March but dropped seven percent against April 1996.
"Despite revenues' increase in real terms, state faces serious problems of financing education system, health service and pensions," Todorovic said.

Another analyst, who asked not to be named, blamed the ruling Socialist authorities for the lack of will to carry out radical reforms and upgrade functioning of the bulky state administration inherited from the former federation.
"There is no readiness to reform in the election year. This is seriously limiting growth and increasing poverty of the people and the entire economy," the analyst said.
